Reproducing Kim et al. (2022) from dandisets 000489 and 000448¶

Paper. Kim V, Semenov I, Kiester AS, Keppler MA, Ibey BL, Bixler JN, Pakhomov AG (2022). Action spectra and mechanisms of (in)efficiency of bipolar electric pulses at electroporation. Bioelectrochemistry 149:108319. doi:10.1016/j.bioelechem.2022.108319. The claims file (claims/kim-2022.yaml) was written from the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC9729435); the paper has no supplement and links no code.

Dandisets. DANDI:000489 version 0.230518.1811 and DANDI:000448 version 0.230421.1844. The paper cites no version of either. Each dandiset has one published version, the one pinned; the drafts list the same assets as the published versions (compared by path and asset identifier, printed below), so the published versions are the most recent content and match the claims file's description as well as the drafts do.

What the dandisets hold. 000489 holds 17 stitched dish images of the Fig. 2 experiment (BPAE cells, 5 pulses of 600 ns or 600+600 ns at 1 Hz, second phase 0, 25, 50, 75 or 100%) and one sample image labelled Fig1F. 000448 holds strobe image stacks of 9 CHO cells (5 unipolar, 4 bipolar; two trials each) given 5 pulses at 833 kHz (Fig. 7); the paper used 18 and 17 cells. Neither holds the experiments of Figs. 3 to 6 or the thermometry of Fig. 1E. Dandisets 000548, 000549 and 000550 of the same lab name this paper and match Figs. 3, 4 and 6 by title; they are not among the paper's datasets that this attempt tests (papers/datasets/kim-2022.yaml), so the claims on Figs. 3 to 6 are blocked here as resting on datasets not used.

Inputs from outside the dandisets. None. The field strength of each ROI, which the paper took from a finite element model whose output is not deposited, is computed here from the geometry in Methods 2.3 (helper kim2022.field_kv_cm).

The Fig. 7 claims are tested first, as their data load in two minutes; the dish images take about six.

Data check: dandiset 000448 (strobe imaging, Fig. 7)¶

Each file holds one trial of one cell (or small group of cells): 500 frames of 512 x 512 pixels. The session description gives the pulse shape and whether the delays were stepped forward (F) or in reverse (R). Methods 2.6: two trials per cell, ascending and descending delays, averaged.

dandiset 000448 description: Time-lapse recordings for the investigation of the relationship between the electroporation efficiency of nsEP and changes in the transmembrane potential (TMP). A strobe imaging synchronized with nsEP exposure was used.  This allowed studying the nanosecond kinetics of TMP charging and relaxation, which is the primary effect of nsEP that rapidly charges the plasma membrane. The methodology involved pulsed laser fluorescence microscopy with voltage-sensitive FluoVolt dye-loaded cells that respond to TMP changes within nanoseconds. FluoVolt has a high sensitivity of about 10 % deltaF/F per 100 mV. During the imaging, a single short pulse laser flash is delivered at a precise time interval (addition of 25ns in each frame) before, during, or after nsEP exposure. The camera shutter opens in advance of and closes after the laser flash, capturing one TMP image per nsEP exposure. Supported by NIH 1R21EY034258

The frame-averaged signal falls with the frame index in both F and R files, so the frames are stored in acquisition order: an R file holds the delays in descending order and is reversed before averaging. The two trials of a cell are then aligned by the lag that best correlates their upper-minus-lower pole signals (the absolute delay of the first frame is not in the files), and averaged.

The paper imaged "individual cells or small groups of cells" (Methods 2.6). In the mask figure below the largest connected group spans touching cells in several recordings, and the pole regions then include some membrane that faces a neighbouring cell. A second figure shows a variant that keeps only the pole pixels with no other part of the group beyond them along the field axis; the share of pole pixels it keeps per file is printed under it, and the Fig. 7 sections give results under it.

def build_cells(key="traces_85_45"):
    """Per cell: F and R trials, R reversed, dark frames removed, R aligned to F,
    averaged; returns the averaged upper and lower ratio traces and the lag."""
    cells = {}
    for c in sorted(st_meta.cell.unique()):
        tr = {}
        for s in strobe:
            if s["cell"] != c:
                continue
            t = s[key]
            dk = k.dark_frames(t["whole"])
            u = np.where(dk, np.nan, t["upper"]).astype(float)
            l = np.where(dk, np.nan, t["lower"]).astype(float)
            if s["recording"] == "reverse":
                u, l = u[::-1], l[::-1]
            tr[s["recording"]] = (u, l, s["pulse_shape"])
        uf, lf, shape = tr["forward"]
        ur, lr, _ = tr["reverse"]
        lag = k.align_lag(uf - lf, ur - lr)
        ur, lr = k.shift(ur, lag), k.shift(lr, lag)
        cells[c] = {"shape": shape, "lag": lag, "uf": uf, "lf": lf, "ur": ur, "lr": lr,
                    "u": np.nanmean([uf, ur], axis=0), "l": np.nanmean([lf, lr], axis=0)}
    return cells

cells = build_cells()
print("lag of the reversed R trial relative to F (frames):", {c: v["lag"] for c, v in cells.items()})

# Pulse onset. The files do not give the delay of each frame. The onset is found on
# the forward trials: the first frame where the mean over unipolar cells of
# (upper - lower) / its baseline rises above the mean + 5 SD of frames 1-30.
uni = [c for c in cells if cells[c]["shape"] == "unipolar"]
bip = [c for c in cells if cells[c]["shape"] == "bipolar"]
d = np.nanmean([(cells[c]["uf"] - cells[c]["lf"]) for c in uni], axis=0)
base = d[1:31]
ONSET = int(np.nonzero(d > np.nanmean(base) + 5 * np.nanstd(base))[0][0])
print("pulse onset frame (forward trials):", ONSET, "=", ONSET * 25, "ns after the first frame")
# Methods 2.6: the mean of the 40 datapoints before the pulse is 100%
B0, B1 = ONSET - 40, ONSET

def pct(x):
    return (x / np.nanmean(x[B0:B1]) - 1) * 100

for c in cells:
    cells[c]["U"] = pct(cells[c]["u"])
    cells[c]["L"] = pct(cells[c]["l"])
    cells[c]["UF"], cells[c]["LF"] = pct(cells[c]["uf"]), pct(cells[c]["lf"])
    cells[c]["UR"], cells[c]["LR"] = pct(cells[c]["ur"]), pct(cells[c]["lr"])
print("baseline frames", B0, "to", B1 - 1)

# Clock check: the response must start at the same frame in both trials of each
# cell (after alignment), and the pulse period must be 1.2 us = 48 frames. The
# autocorrelation of the mean unipolar upper-minus-lower trace, after the onset,
# gives the period.
t_ns = (np.arange(500) - ONSET) * 25.0
for c in cells:
    for tag in ["UF", "UR"]:
        x = cells[c][tag] - cells[c]["L" + tag[1]]
        b = x[B0:B1]
        on = np.nonzero(x[B0:] > np.nanmean(b) + 5 * np.nanstd(b))[0]
        cells[c]["on_" + tag] = int(on[0] + B0) if len(on) else None
print("onset frame per cell and trial:", {c: (cells[c]["on_UF"], cells[c]["on_UR"]) for c in cells})
x = np.nanmean([cells[c]["U"] - cells[c]["L"] for c in uni], axis=0)[ONSET:ONSET + 240]
x = x - x.mean()
ac = [np.sum(x[:-lag] * x[lag:]) for lag in range(20, 80)]
print("period of the unipolar response (frames):", 20 + int(np.argmax(ac)), "(expected 48 = 1200 ns / 25 ns)")
# which pole rises during the first pulse, per cell
for c in cells:
    w = slice(ONSET + 12, ONSET + 24)

Every cell's upper pole (smaller row index) rises and its lower pole falls during the first pulse, so the field axis is the image's vertical axis in every file and the orientation is the same in all cells, as expected for a fixed rig. FluoVolt emission rises with depolarization (the dandiset's description, printed in the data check, gives a sensitivity of about 10% dF/F per 100 mV, and the paper's Fig. 7 plots depolarization at the cathode-facing pole as a positive change); the cathode-facing pole is therefore the upper pole, and the anode-facing pole the lower one. The files do not say where the electrodes were relative to the image, so this rests on the dye's sign.

fig7-unipolar-pole-polarization¶

Unipolar 600 ns pulses depolarized the membrane quickly at the cathode-facing pole of the cell and hyperpolarized it in mirror image at the anode-facing pole.

Criterion: at the end of the first pulse (600 ns) the cathodic and anodic values differ from zero in opposite directions (one-sample t-test across cells, p < 0.05), and the anodic magnitude is within half to twice the cathodic. The value at 600 ns is the frame 24 steps after the onset; the mean of frames 500-600 ns is a variant.

In [9]:
def at(c, pole, t):
    return cells[c][pole][ONSET + int(round(t / 25))]

def win(c, pole, t0, t1):
    return np.nanmean(cells[c][pole][ONSET + int(t0 / 25):ONSET + int(t1 / 25) + 1])

def unipolar_polarization(key_cells):
    rows = []
    for label, f in [("value at 600 ns", lambda c, p: at(c, p, 600)), ("mean 500-600 ns", lambda c, p: win(c, p, 500, 600))]:
        ca = np.array([f(c, CATH) for c in key_cells])
        an = np.array([f(c, ANOD) for c in key_cells])
        tc, ta = stats.ttest_1samp(ca, 0), stats.ttest_1samp(an, 0)
        ratio = abs(an.mean()) / abs(ca.mean())
        ok = (tc.pvalue < 0.05) and (ta.pvalue < 0.05) and np.sign(ca.mean()) != np.sign(an.mean()) and 0.5 <= ratio <= 2
        rows.append({"reading": label, "cathodic mean %": ca.mean(), "cathodic p": tc.pvalue, "anodic mean %": an.mean(),
                     "anodic p": ta.pvalue, "|anodic|/|cathodic|": ratio, "n cells": len(key_cells), "criterion met": ok})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

r_pol = unipolar_polarization(uni)
print(r_pol.to_string())
print("per cell, value at 600 ns (cathodic, anodic):", {c: (round(at(c, CATH, 600), 1), round(at(c, ANOD, 600), 1)) for c in uni})

    print(f"pole variant {key}: cathodic {ca.mean():+.1f}% (p={stats.ttest_1samp(ca,0).pvalue:.2g}), anodic {an.mean():+.1f}% (p={stats.ttest_1samp(an,0).pvalue:.2g}), ratio {abs(an.mean())/abs(ca.mean()):.2f}")

Result: reproduced, resting on assumptions. At the end of the first pulse the cathode-facing pole is +22.1% (p = 0.0012) and the anode-facing pole -20.7% (p = 0.0026) over 5 unipolar cells, opposite in sign, with a magnitude ratio of 0.94; the 500 to 600 ns mean and five variants of the pole regions give the same (ratios 0.90 to 1.05, all p <= 0.013), among them the regions that leave out membrane facing a neighbouring cell (+22.1% and -20.4%, ratio 0.92). Every cell shows the same orientation. Which pole faces the cathode rests on FluoVolt brightening with depolarization, as the files do not record the electrode positions, and the pole regions are an assumption. The paper used 18 cells; 5 are in the dandiset.

fig7-charging-time-constant¶

Fitting the cathodic pole response to the first unipolar pulse gave a charging time constant of 200 ns and a maximum polarization of 31% emission change (425 points, r = 0.93, p < 0.0001), and the discharge after it a time constant of 520 ns from 31.5% (425 points, r = 0.85, p < 0.0001).

Charging, A (1 - exp(-t/tau)) over 0 to 600 ns of the first pulse (25 frames, t = 0 at the onset frame); discharge, A exp(-t/tau) over 600 to 1175 ns, t from the end of the pulse (24 frames; the frame at 1200 ns is the onset frame of the next pulse, already rising). Readings (a) the points of every cell pooled, (b) the trace averaged over cells. The correlation coefficient is that between the points and the fit.

In [10]:
def fit_pulse(grp, pulse=0, pole=CATH, free=False):
    t0 = ONSET + pulse * 48
    tc = np.arange(0, 25) * 25.0          # frames 0..24 of the pulse: 0 to 600 ns (criterion)
    td = np.arange(0, 24) * 25.0          # frames 24..47: 600 to 1175 ns, t from pulse end
    res = {}
    for reading in ["pooled", "mean"]:
        if reading == "pooled":
            vc = np.concatenate([cells[c][pole][t0:t0 + 25] for c in grp]); tcc = np.tile(tc, len(grp))
            vd = np.concatenate([cells[c][pole][t0 + 24:t0 + 48] for c in grp]); tdd = np.tile(td, len(grp))
        else:
            vc = np.nanmean([cells[c][pole][t0:t0 + 25] for c in grp], axis=0); tcc = tc
            vd = np.nanmean([cells[c][pole][t0 + 24:t0 + 48] for c in grp], axis=0); tdd = td
        okc, okd = np.isfinite(vc), np.isfinite(vd)
        if free:
            pc, fc = k.charge_fit_free(tcc[okc], vc[okc]); A, tau_c = pc[0], pc[2]
        else:
            pc, fc = k.charge_fit(tcc[okc], vc[okc]); A, tau_c = pc
        pd_, fd = k.discharge_fit(tdd[okd], vd[okd])
        rc = stats.pearsonr(vc[okc], fc); rd = stats.pearsonr(vd[okd], fd)
        res[reading + "_fit"] = (tcc[okc], vc[okc], fc, tdd[okd], vd[okd], fd)
        res[reading] = {"tau_charge_ns": tau_c, "A_charge_%": A, "r_charge": rc[0], "p_charge": rc[1], "n_charge": int(okc.sum()),
                        "tau_discharge_ns": pd_[1], "A_discharge_%": pd_[0], "r_discharge": rd[0], "p_discharge": rd[1], "n_discharge": int(okd.sum())}
    fits = {r: res.pop(r + "_fit") for r in ("pooled", "mean")}
    out = pd.DataFrame(res).T
    out.attrs["fits"] = fits
    return out

    print(f"cell {c}: tau charge {f1.tau_charge_ns:.0f} ns, A {f1['A_charge_%']:.1f}%, tau discharge {f1.tau_discharge_ns:.0f} ns, A {f1['A_discharge_%']:.1f}%")

Result: not reproduced, resting on assumptions. Over the 5 unipolar cells the charging fit over 0 to 600 ns gives tau = 191 ns (within 180 to 220 ns) but a maximum of 23.2% (expected 31 +- 3.1%); the discharge fit gives tau = 613 ns (expected 520 +- 52 ns) from 22.7% (expected 31.5 +- 3.15%). The pooled points (125 and 120) and the mean trace give the same parameters; r = 0.84 and 0.64 for the pooled points (p < 1e-14), 0.998 and 0.997 for the mean trace, whose residuals are at most 1.4 points (RMS 0.51 and 0.33). The discharge constant is 3.2 times the charging constant, against the paper's 2.5. The charging tau is not robust to the onset: moving the onset by one frame gives 149 to 249 ns, and placing t = 0 half a frame earlier 216 ns; the discharge tau stays at 615 to 627 ns and the amplitudes at 21.9 to 24.7%, outside tolerance in every case, so the outcome does not depend on the onset. The dandiset holds 5 of the paper's 18 unipolar cells, and the per-cell amplitudes range from 14.4 to 31.3%, so the smaller amplitude may come from the subset or from the pole regions assumed here. Leaving out the pole membrane that faces a neighbouring cell does not change it (A = 23.2% and 22.8%, tau = 191 and 614 ns).

fig7-later-pulses-same-tau-difference¶

Fits to the later pulses of the unipolar train gave the same kind of difference between charging and discharging time constants as the first pulse.

The fits of fig7-charging-time-constant, with the criterion's A (1 - exp(-t/tau)), are repeated for pulses 2 to 5; the discharge after pulse 5 is fitted over the same span as the others. Pulses 2 to 5 start from a charged membrane (Results 3.5, "charging by the subsequent pulses ... started with the partially charged membrane"), which that form cannot follow; a charging fit with a free starting value, V0 + (A - V0)(1 - exp(-t/tau)), is shown as a variant.

Result: partially reproduced, resting on assumptions. With the criterion's A (1 - exp(-t/tau)) form the discharge constant exceeds the charging constant for all four later pulses, with ratios of 7.9 to 10.5: none within 2.25 to 2.75 or within 10% of the first pulse's 3.22 (2.90 to 3.54). With the free-start variant the ratios are 2.99, 3.62, 2.88 and 2.97: the discharge constant is again the larger for all four, none is within 2.25 to 2.75, and pulses 2 and 5 are within 10% of the first pulse's ratio (pulse 4, 2.876, falls just below 2.895). Both forms give partially reproduced.

fig7-bipolar-overshoot¶

Bipolar pulses caused the same initial polarization as unipolar ones during the first phase, followed by a faster discharge and an overshoot into the opposite polarity.

In [13]:
cu = np.array([at(c, CATH, 600) for c in uni]); cb = np.array([at(c, CATH, 600) for c in bip])
t_i = stats.ttest_ind(cb, cu)
gap = abs(cb.mean() - cu.mean()) > (stats.sem(cb) + stats.sem(cu))
print(f"(i) cathodic value at 600 ns: bipolar {cb.mean():.1f}% (n={len(cb)}), unipolar {cu.mean():.1f}% (n={len(cu)}); "
      f"difference {cb.mean()-cu.mean():+.1f}%, unpaired t-test p = {t_i.pvalue:.3g}; error-bar gap rule says different: {gap}")
mu = np.nanmean([cells[c][CATH] for c in uni], axis=0); mb_ = np.nanmean([cells[c][CATH] for c in bip], axis=0)
def first_return(m, frac):
    pk = m[ONSET + 24]
    after = np.nonzero(m[ONSET + 24:ONSET + 48] <= frac * pk)[0]
    return after[0] * 25 if len(after) else None
for frac in (0.5, 0.1, 0.0):
    print(f"(ii) time after the end of the first phase for the mean trace to fall to {frac:.0%} of its 600 ns value: bipolar {first_return(mb_, frac)} ns, unipolar {first_return(mu, frac)} ns (None: not within 600 ns)")
seg = mb_[ONSET + 24:ONSET + 48]
imin = int(np.nanargmin(seg)); vals = np.array([cells[c][CATH][ONSET + 24 + imin] for c in bip])
t_iii = stats.ttest_1samp(vals, 0)
print(f"(iii) bipolar mean minimum in 600-1200 ns: {seg[imin]:.1f}% at {600 + imin*25} ns; cell values {np.round(vals,1).tolist()}, one-sample t p = {t_iii.pvalue:.3g}")
print("per bipolar cell, minimum in 600-1200 ns:", {c: round(float(np.nanmin(cells[c][CATH][ONSET + 24:ONSET + 48])), 1) for c in bip})
# variant: the value at a time fixed before looking at the data, the last frame of the second phase (1175 ns)
v_end = np.array([cells[c][CATH][ONSET + 47] for c in bip])
print(f"(iii) variant, value at 1175 ns (end of the second phase): {v_end.mean():.1f}%, cells {np.round(v_end, 1).tolist()}, one-sample t p = {stats.ttest_1samp(v_end, 0).pvalue:.3g}")

(i) cathodic value at 600 ns: bipolar 21.5% (n=4), unipolar 22.1% (n=5); difference -0.6%, unpaired t-test p = 0.855; error-bar gap rule says different: False
(ii) time after the end of the first phase for the mean trace to fall to 50% of its 600 ns value: bipolar 150 ns, unipolar 475 ns (None: not within 600 ns)
(ii) time after the end of the first phase for the mean trace to fall to 10% of its 600 ns value: bipolar 275 ns, unipolar None ns (None: not within 600 ns)
(ii) time after the end of the first phase for the mean trace to fall to 0% of its 600 ns value: bipolar 325 ns, unipolar None ns (None: not within 600 ns)
(iii) bipolar mean minimum in 600-1200 ns: -8.1% at 1175 ns; cell values [-6.7, -7.7, -9.9, -8.2], one-sample t p = 0.00124
per bipolar cell, minimum in 600-1200 ns: {'cell09': -6.7, 'cell12': -7.8, 'cell19': -10.6, 'cell23': -8.2}
(iii) variant, value at 1175 ns (end of the second phase): -8.1%, cells [-6.7, -7.7, -9.9, -8.2], one-sample t p = 0.00124

Result: reproduced, resting on assumptions. (i) At 600 ns the cathodic pole is 21.5% after bipolar pulses (4 cells) and 22.1% after unipolar pulses (5 cells), p = 0.855, and the error-bar gap rule finds no difference. (ii) After the first phase the bipolar mean falls to half its value in 150 ns against 475 ns for unipolar pulses, and to zero in 325 ns, which the unipolar trace does not reach before the next pulse. (iii) The bipolar mean reaches -8.1% at 1175 ns; the four cell values (-6.7 to -9.9%) differ from zero, p = 0.0012. That time was chosen on the mean of the same cells; the last frame of the second phase, a time fixed in advance, is the same frame and gives the same result. Four of the paper's 17 bipolar cells are in the dandiset.

fig7-bipolar-alternation¶

In 833 kHz trains, bipolar pulses caused the membrane potential to alternate repeatedly between positive and negative values.

In [14]:
alt = []
for p in range(5):
    t0 = ONSET + p * 48
    end1 = np.array([cells[c][CATH][t0 + 24] for c in bip])
    mseg = np.nanmean([cells[c][CATH][t0 + 24:t0 + 48] for c in bip], axis=0)
    im = int(np.nanargmin(mseg))
    mins = np.array([cells[c][CATH][t0 + 24 + im] for c in bip])
    a, b = stats.ttest_1samp(end1, 0), stats.ttest_1samp(mins, 0)
    alt.append({"pulse": p + 1, "end of phase 1 %": end1.mean(), "p": a.pvalue, "phase 2 minimum %": mins.mean(), "at ns": 600 + im * 25,
                "p ": b.pvalue, "both significant, right signs": end1.mean() > 0 and mins.mean() < 0 and a.pvalue < 0.05 and b.pvalue < 0.05})
alt = pd.DataFrame(alt)
print(alt.round(4).to_string())
print("pulses meeting the criterion:", int(alt.iloc[:, -1].sum()), "of 5; n =", len(bip), "cells")
# variant: phase 2 value at a fixed time, the last frame before the next pulse (1175 ns into each period)
ends = np.array([[cells[c][CATH][ONSET + p * 48 + 47] for c in bip] for p in range(5)])
print("variant, value at 1175 ns of each period:", [f"pulse {p + 1}: {ends[p].mean():.1f}% (p = {stats.ttest_1samp(ends[p], 0).pvalue:.2g})" for p in range(5)])

Result: reproduced, resting on assumptions. For each of the five pulses, the cathodic pole is positive at the end of the first phase (19.3 to 21.5%, p <= 0.0001) and negative at its second phase minimum (-8.1 to -9.1%, p <= 0.0013), over 4 bipolar cells. The time of the minimum is taken from the mean of the same cells; the value at 1175 ns of each period, fixed in advance, gives -8.1 to -9.1% with p <= 0.0017.

fig7-summation-without-buildup¶

With 600 ns unipolar pulses at 833 kHz, each pulse charged the membrane to the same peak, with no stepwise build-up; the pulses merged into a continuous sawtooth polarization.

In [15]:
peaks = np.array([[cells[c][CATH][ONSET + p * 48 + 24] for p in range(5)] for c in uni])
pre = np.array([[cells[c][CATH][ONSET + p * 48 - 1] for p in range(1, 5)] for c in uni])
rows = []
for p in range(1, 5):
    tu = stats.ttest_ind(peaks[:, p], peaks[:, 0]); tp = stats.ttest_rel(peaks[:, p], peaks[:, 0])
    tpre = stats.ttest_1samp(pre[:, p - 1], 0)
    rows.append({"pulse": p + 1, "peak %": peaks[:, p].mean(), "peak - first": peaks[:, p].mean() - peaks[:, 0].mean(),
                 "unpaired p": tu.pvalue, "paired p (variant)": tp.pvalue, "value before pulse %": pre[:, p - 1].mean(), "p vs 0": tpre.pvalue})
summ = pd.DataFrame(rows)
summ["peak - first, % of first"] = summ["peak - first"] / peaks[:, 0].mean() * 100
print("first peak: %.1f%%" % peaks[:, 0].mean())
print(summ.round(4).to_string())
# peak taken as the maximum within each pulse (variant)
pk2 = np.array([[np.nanmax(cells[c][CATH][ONSET + p * 48:ONSET + p * 48 + 25]) for p in range(5)] for c in uni])
print("variant, maximum within each pulse:", pk2.mean(0).round(1), "unpaired p vs first:", [round(stats.ttest_ind(pk2[:, p], pk2[:, 0]).pvalue, 3) for p in range(1, 5)])

Result: reproduced, resting on assumptions. The peaks of pulses 2 to 5 (23.4 to 24.3%) do not differ from the first (22.1%) by the unpaired test the criterion names (p = 0.61 to 0.75), and the trace before each of pulses 2 to 5 stays above rest (8.8 to 9.9%, p = 0.009 to 0.017), over 5 unipolar cells. The paired variant finds the later peaks 1.4 to 2.2 points higher, with p < 0.05 for pulses 2 to 4 (p = 0.014 to 0.040), a build-up of 7.8 to 10.1% of the first peak within cells; pulse 5 is 6.1% higher (p = 0.089). With 5 cells, the absence found by the unpaired test is weak evidence.

Data check: dandiset 000489 (dish images, Fig. 2)¶

Each file holds one stitched image of a whole dish, 22323 x 22323 pixels with two channels. The images are streamed in bands and reduced to 7 x 7 pixel block means as they load (4 dishes at a time); everything below works on the block means.

import re
def amp_of(d):
    m = re.match(r"Fig2_(\d+)_", d["subject_id"] + "_")
    return int(m.group(1)) if m else None
for d in dishes:
    d["amp"] = amp_of(d)

In every Fig. 2 dish channel index 1 is brighter between the electrodes than 3 mm away along bb' (1.28 to 6.54 times, below 3 in 10 of 17 dishes) and more so than index 0 (1.02 to 1.45 times), so index 1 is YO-PRO-1 and index 0 MemBrite. The series description of the 17 Fig. 2 files names "Channel1" for both filter sets and for MemBrite, which does not say which index holds which dye, and describes 144 images (12 x 12 grid) of a well of a six-well plate, where Methods 2.5 describes 35 mm dishes. The three 25% files name their series "Fig2_25" without the dish number. The images are stored with conversion 1.0 and offset 0 and no resolution (-1). The two channels of the Fig1F sample image are the same image (same digest). The electrode spacing measured at 0.65 um per pixel agrees with the 4.5 mm of Methods 2.2, which supports the pixel size (the files give none).

The YP channel of sub-Fig2-0-03 (unipolar) and sub-Fig2-25-04 (25% bipolar) is the same image, block for block, while their MemBrite channels differ, and the two files give different session dates (2021-07-29 and 2021-07-26). One recording was deposited under two dishes, and nothing says which dish it belongs to. The main analysis counts it once by leaving out both dishes (unipolar and 25% then have 2 dishes each); the variants assign the shared image to the unipolar group or to the 25% group.

Field model and ROI¶

The field of each ROI comes from the two-cylinder solution in the helper (the geometry of Methods 2.3, 5.75 kV). It gives 15.38 kV/cm at the centre, against the 15.1 kV/cm the paper's finite element model gives there (Results 3.1 and Fig. 2C legend): 1.8% higher. The named fields 15.1, 8.7 and 6.7 kV/cm are taken at the ROI whose model field is closest, scaled by 15.1/15.38 (the paper's value at the centre); this scaling does not change which ROI is closest.

In [20]:
def long_table(key="rois", assign=None):
    """One row per dish and ROI. assign: None (leave out the duplicated pair),
    0 or 25 (use the shared YP image once, under that amplitude)."""
    rows = []
    for d in fig2:
        if d["subject_id"] in ("Fig2_0_03", "Fig2_25_04"):
            if assign is None:
                continue
            if (assign == 0) != (d["subject_id"] == "Fig2_0_03"):
                continue
        for r in d[key]:
            rows.append({"dish": d["subject_id"], "amp": d["amp"], **r})
    t = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    t["field"] = t.field_kv_cm * 15.1 / fields[0]
    t["abs_off"] = t.offset_mm.abs().round(1)
    return t

def per_dish(t, reading="a"):
    """Dish value per distance from the centre: (a) mean of the two ROI at +-offset,
    (b+) the positive side only, (b-) the negative side only."""
    if reading == "a":
        s = t
    elif reading == "b+":
        s = t[t.offset_mm >= 0]
    else:
        s = t[t.offset_mm <= 0]
    g = s.groupby(["amp", "dish", "abs_off"]).agg(YP=("YP", "mean"), field=("field", "mean")).reset_index()
    return g

T = {None: long_table(), 0: long_table(assign=0), 25: long_table(assign=25)}
D = {(a, r): per_dish(T[a], r) for a in T for r in ["a", "b+", "b-"]}
main = D[(None, "a")]

fig2a-uptake-rises-with-field¶

For unipolar 600 ns pulses and for bipolar 600+600 ns pulses with every second phase amplitude, a train of 5 pulses at 1 Hz evoked YP uptake that increased with the local electric field strength.

Strongest-field ROI (centre) against weakest-field ROI (3.0 mm, 5.0 kV/cm, the outermost ROI of the set used here), dish values, two-sided t-test unpaired and paired. The ROI set's outer limit is not given by the paper (its figure range is in the PDF only); the ROI at 2.4 mm (6.6 kV/cm) is shown as a variant weakest ROI.

In [23]:
def rises(g, weak=3.0):
    out = []
    for a in [0, 25, 50, 75, 100]:
        s = g[g.amp == a].pivot(index="dish", columns="abs_off", values="YP")
        hi, lo = s[0.0], s[weak]
        tu = stats.ttest_ind(hi, lo); tp = stats.ttest_rel(hi, lo)
        m = s.mean()
        rho = stats.spearmanr(g[g.amp == a].groupby("abs_off").field.mean(), m)
        out.append({"amp %": a, "n": len(s), "YP strongest": hi.mean(), "YP weakest": lo.mean(), "unpaired p": tu.pvalue,
                    "paired p": tp.pvalue, "higher & p<0.05 (unpaired)": hi.mean() > lo.mean() and tu.pvalue < 0.05,
                    "higher & p<0.05 (paired)": hi.mean() > lo.mean() and tp.pvalue < 0.05, "Spearman rho (means vs field)": rho[0], "rho p": rho[1]})
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

for (a, r), g in D.items():
    for weak in (3.0, 2.4):
        res = rises(g, weak)
        tag = f"duplicate {'left out' if a is None else 'as ' + str(a) + '%'}, reading ({r}), weakest ROI at {weak} mm"
        print(tag, "| amplitudes passing, unpaired:", int(res.iloc[:, 6].sum()), "paired:", int(res.iloc[:, 7].sum()))
        if (a, r, weak) == (None, "a", 3.0):
            main_rises = res
print()
print(main_rises.round(4).to_string())

Result: reproduced, resting on an assumption. With the two dishes that share one YP image left out, YP is higher at the strongest field than at the weakest ROI for all five amplitudes with p < 0.05 by the unpaired test (p = 0.0001 to 0.044), and the Spearman correlation of mean YP with field is 0.96 to 0.99. By the paired test 3 of 5 pass (unipolar and 25%, with 2 dishes each, give p = 0.12 and 0.13). Every ROI reading and the weaker ROI at 2.4 mm give the same counts. Assigning the shared image to the unipolar or the 25% group gives 4 of 5 (unpaired). The outcome takes the unpaired test, the two-sample test that the Methods' name denotes, as an assumption.

fig2a-vertical-scales¶

The vertical scale of the Fig. 2A panels goes from 1200 a.u. for unipolar pulses down to only 250 a.u. for bipolar pulses with a 75% second phase.

The image values are 16-bit counts with no conversion (conversion 1.0, offset 0 in every file, printed in the data check); nothing shows that they were rescaled on export, and the footprint levels (YP0 of 177 to 295 counts) are plausible camera counts. They are taken as the units the paper measured, which the data are consistent with but cannot prove.

Result: not reproduced, resting on an assumption. The largest unipolar mean is 651 a.u. (mean + s.e.m. 754, below 1200, and above 250), but for 75% bipolar pulses the largest mean is 263 a.u. and the largest mean + s.e.m. 339 a.u., above 250, under every reading (311 to 372). This takes the image counts as the paper's units, which the files are consistent with but do not state. The unit-free ratio of the largest unipolar and 75% means is 2.47 (1.74 to 2.50 over the readings), against 4.8 for the paper's axis limits; axis limits only bound the data, so the ratio points the same way without deciding it.

fig2b-exponential-same-slope¶

YP uptake increased exponentially with the field strength, and the second phase did not change the slope of the exponential fits on a semi-log scale.

Fits to the mean values over ROI at or above the cutoff: YP = A exp(kE) by nonlinear least squares, against a straight line. Per-dish fits give a slope k per dish; each bipolar amplitude is compared with the unipolar slopes by an unpaired two-sided t-test. The outcome changes with the cutoff and the fit method, so a reading is adopted, as an assumption: the criterion's main reading, 8 kV/cm (the top of the legend's "6-8 kV/cm", which leaves out what every amplitude leaves out) and nonlinear least squares on linear YP (the values the legend plots). 7 and 6 kV/cm and linear regression of log YP on field (ROI with YP <= 0 dropped) are shown as variants.

In [25]:
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
expf = lambda E, A, kk: A * np.exp(kk * E)

def fit_exp(E, Y):
    try:
        p, cov = curve_fit(expf, E, Y, p0=[max(np.mean(Y), 1) * np.exp(-0.2 * np.mean(E)), 0.2], maxfev=20000)
        return p, np.sqrt(np.diag(cov)), np.sum((Y - expf(E, *p)) ** 2)
    except Exception as e:
        return None, None, np.nan

def fig2b(g, cut, method="nls"):
    rows, slopes = [], {}
    for a in [0, 25, 50, 75, 100]:
        s = g[(g.amp == a) & (g.field >= cut)]
        m = s.groupby("abs_off").agg(E=("field", "mean"), Y=("YP", "mean"))
        lin = np.polyfit(m.E, m.Y, 1); rss_lin = np.sum((m.Y - np.polyval(lin, m.E)) ** 2)
        p, se, rss_exp = fit_exp(m.E.values, m.Y.values)
        ks = []
        for dish, sd in s.groupby("dish"):
            if method == "nls":
                pp, _, _ = fit_exp(sd.field.values, sd.YP.values)
                ks.append(pp[1] if pp is not None else np.nan)
            else:
                ok = sd.YP > 0
                ks.append(np.polyfit(sd.field[ok], np.log(sd.YP[ok]), 1)[0] if ok.sum() >= 3 else np.nan)
        slopes[a] = np.array(ks)
        rows.append({"amp %": a, "ROI": len(m), "k of fit to means (1/(kV/cm))": p[1] if p is not None else np.nan,
                     "k se": se[1] if se is not None else np.nan, "RSS exp": rss_exp, "RSS line": rss_lin, "exp better": rss_exp < rss_lin,
                     "per-dish k": np.round(slopes[a], 3).tolist()})
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    out["k ratio to unipolar"] = out["k of fit to means (1/(kV/cm))"] / out.loc[0, "k of fit to means (1/(kV/cm))"]
    ps = {}
    for a in [25, 50, 75, 100]:
        x, y = slopes[a][np.isfinite(slopes[a])], slopes[0][np.isfinite(slopes[0])]
        ps[a] = stats.ttest_ind(x, y).pvalue if len(x) > 1 and len(y) > 1 else np.nan
    out["p slope vs unipolar"] = out["amp %"].map(ps)
    return out

for cut in (8, 7, 6):
    for method in ("nls", "log-linear"):
        for key in [(None, "a"), (0, "a"), (25, "a")]:
            r = fig2b(D[key], cut, method)
            nexp = int(r["exp better"].sum()); ndiff = int((r["p slope vs unipolar"] < 0.05).sum())
            print(f"cutoff {cut} kV/cm, per-dish {method}, duplicate {'left out' if key[0] is None else 'as ' + str(key[0]) + '%'}: exp better for {nexp}/5;"
                  f" bipolar slopes differing from unipolar (p<0.05): {ndiff}/4; p = {r['p slope vs unipolar'].dropna().round(3).tolist()}")
            if (cut, method, key) == (8, "nls", (None, "a")):
                main_2b = r

Result: partially reproduced, resting on an assumption. Under the adopted reading (8 kV/cm, nonlinear least squares) the exponential fits the means better than a line for 3 of 5 amplitudes (unipolar and 50% are better fitted by a line), short of the four the criterion needs, and no bipolar slope from the per-dish fits differs from the unipolar slopes (p = 0.12 to 0.80). One part of the claim holds and the other does not; the criterion does not name an outcome for this case, and partially reproduced is used. The slope test has little power: the unipolar group has 2 dishes (k = 0.205 and 0.41). The slopes of the fits to the means are 0.189 +- 0.016 (50%) and 0.191 +- 0.014 (75%) against 0.263 +- 0.027 for unipolar, 0.72 times; 25% and 100% give 0.88 and 1.07 times. Under the variants the outcome changes: at 7 kV/cm the exponential is better for 4 of 5 and at 6 kV/cm for 5 of 5, with no slope differing by the nonlinear fits (reproduced), while the log-linear fits at 7 and 6 kV/cm find all 4 bipolar slopes different (p = 0.004 to 0.042, not reproduced) when the shared image is left out.

fig2c-max-inhibition-50-75¶

The strongest inhibition of YP uptake, to about 20% of the uptake after unipolar pulses, was reached with a second phase of 50 to 75% of the first (p < 0.01).

Percent of unipolar YP at each ROI with field 8.7 to 15.1 kV/cm (scaled fields; the ROI at 0 to 1.8 mm). Ordering: the lower of 50% and 75% below 25% and 100% at every such field. "~20%": (a) the mean over those fields for the better of 50 and 75%, (b) the lowest percent at any of them. Tests, unpaired: (i) 50% and 75% dish YP against unipolar, (ii) 50% and 75% against 25% and 100%, at each field.

rng = sorted(main.abs_off[(main.field >= 8.7 - 1e-9) & (main.field <= 15.1 + 1e-9)].unique())
print("ROI in 8.7 to 15.1 kV/cm (offsets, mm):", rng, "| scaled fields:", [round(float(scaled[list(offs).index(o)]), 2) for o in rng])

def fig2c(g):
    m = g.groupby(["amp", "abs_off"]).YP.mean().unstack(0)
    pc = (m.div(m[0], axis=0) * 100).loc[rng]
    order = ((pc[[50, 75]].min(axis=1) < pc[25]) & (pc[[50, 75]].min(axis=1) < pc[100]))
    best = 50 if pc[50].mean() <= pc[75].mean() else 75
    ra, rb = pc[best].mean(), pc[[50, 75]].min(axis=1).min()
    ti, tii = [], []
    for o in rng:
        v = {a: g[(g.amp == a) & (g.abs_off == o)].YP.values for a in [0, 25, 50, 75, 100]}
        ti.append({a: stats.ttest_ind(v[a], v[0]).pvalue for a in (50, 75)})
        tii.append({(a, b): stats.ttest_ind(v[a], v[b]).pvalue for a in (50, 75) for b in (25, 100)})
    ti, tii = pd.DataFrame(ti, index=rng), pd.DataFrame(tii, index=rng)
    return pc, order, best, ra, rb, ti, tii

          f" p<0.01 at {int(f_i.sum())}/{len(rng)} fields by (i), {int(f_ii.sum())}/{len(rng)} by (ii), {int((f_i | f_ii).sum())}/{len(rng)} by either;"

Result: not reproduced, resting on an assumption. At every ROI from 8.78 to 15.1 kV/cm the lower of the 50% and 75% values is below the 25% and 100% values (10 of 10). The best amplitude, 50%, gives 49.3% of unipolar on average (reading a) and 35.1% at its lowest (reading b), both outside 20 +- 2%. The p < 0.01 test does not hold at every field under either comparison: (ii), the better of 50 or 75% against both 25% and 100%, at 7 of 10 fields, and (i), against unipolar with 2 unipolar dishes, at 3 of 10. The criterion runs the test at each field and does not say at how many it must hold; it is taken to hold, like the ordering, at every field (an assumption). No variant reaches every field (at most 7 of 10 by either comparison). If holding at most fields sufficed, the outcome would be partially reproduced. Averaged over the 10 fields the 25% and 100% pulses give 110.0% and 118.1% of the unipolar value (64 to 168% at single fields), so on average they do not inhibit in these dishes; 25% is below 100% at 7 of 10 fields. The 75% and 100% dishes were imaged on 2021-08-24 and the two unipolar dishes analysed on 2021-07-29, with footprint YP0 of 177 to 227 a.u. against 236 and 292 a.u. (table above).

fig2c-inhibition-flat-above-8-7¶

Between 8.7 and 15.1 kV/cm the degree of inhibition by the second phase did not depend on the field strength.

Each bipolar dish value divided by the unipolar mean at the same ROI; 8.7 kV/cm (ROI at 1.8 mm) against 15.1 kV/cm (centre), unpaired two-sided t-test, p < 0.05. The ROI placement changes the outcome, so a reading is adopted, as an assumption: (a), the ROI on both sides of the centre averaged per dish, as bb' runs from b to b' through the centre (Fig. 1C) and the two halves have the same fields. One side only, (b+) and (b-), and the footprint discs of 0.1 and 0.3 mm are shown as variants.

In [27]:
def ratio_table(g):
    um = g[g.amp == 0].groupby("abs_off").YP.mean()
    r = g[g.amp > 0].copy()
    r["pct"] = r.YP / r.abs_off.map(um) * 100
    return r

o87, o151, o67 = nearest(8.7), nearest(15.1), nearest(6.7)
for label, g in VARIANTS:
    r = ratio_table(g)
    rows = []
    for a in [25, 50, 75, 100]:
        x = r[(r.amp == a) & (r.abs_off == o87)].set_index("dish").pct
        y = r[(r.amp == a) & (r.abs_off == o151)].set_index("dish").pct
        rows.append({"amp %": a, "% at 8.7": x.mean(), "% at 15.1": y.mean(), "difference": x.mean() - y.mean(),
                     "unpaired p": stats.ttest_ind(x, y).pvalue, "paired p (variant)": stats.ttest_rel(x, y.loc[x.index]).pvalue})
    rows = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    # every pair of ROI in the range (variant)
    npairs = nsig = 0
    for a in [25, 50, 75, 100]:
        for i, o1 in enumerate(rng):
            for o2 in rng[i + 1:]:
                npairs += 1
                nsig += stats.ttest_ind(r[(r.amp == a) & (r.abs_off == o1)].pct, r[(r.amp == a) & (r.abs_off == o2)].pct).pvalue < 0.05
    print(f"{label}: amplitudes with p<0.05 (unpaired): {int((rows['unpaired p'] < 0.05).sum())}/4, p = {rows['unpaired p'].round(3).tolist()}, differences {rows['difference'].round(1).tolist()} points;"
          f" every-pair variant: {nsig}/{npairs} pairs differ")
    if label.startswith("duplicate left out, reading (a)"):
        main_flat = rows
print()
print(main_flat.round(4).to_string())

Result: reproduced, resting on an assumption. Under reading (a) no bipolar amplitude differs between 8.78 and 15.1 kV/cm by the unpaired test (p = 0.07 to 0.83), with either assignment of the shared image or footprint disc. The differences are large for 50% (67.8% against 35.1%, +32.7 points, p = 0.072) and 75% (91.5% against 40.0%, +51.5 points, p = 0.15), with 5 and 3 dishes, so the absence rests on few dishes, not on small effects. Under the one-sided readings one amplitude differs (100% under b+, p = 0.033; 50% under b-, p = 0.036), which would make the claim not reproduced. Comparing every pair of ROI in the range, 19 of 180 pairs differ at p < 0.05 under (a), against 9 expected by chance.

fig2c-weaker-at-6-7¶

Inhibition was weaker at 6.7 kV/cm than at the higher field strengths, with p < 0.01 for the 50% bipolar pulses and p < 0.05 for the 100% bipolar pulses.

Percent of the unipolar mean at the ROI closest to 6.7 kV/cm (2.4 mm) against (i) each ROI from 8.7 to 15.1 kV/cm and (ii) those ROI pooled. Pooling is done within each dish (the dish's mean percent over the higher field ROI), so that each dish counts once; pooling every dish and ROI value treats the ROI of one dish as independent and is shown only as a variant. The unpaired test is adopted, as for fig2a-uptake-rises-with-field, and ROI reading (a), as for fig2c-inhibition-flat-above-8-7; the paired test, the one-sided ROI readings and the footprint discs are variants.

# (which treats the ROI of a dish as independent) are shown as variants.
for label, g in VARIANTS:

    lines = []

        x = r[(r.amp == a) & (r.abs_off == o67)].set_index("dish").pct
        higher = [r[(r.amp == a) & (r.abs_off == o)].set_index("dish").pct for o in rng]
        each_u = [stats.ttest_ind(x, h).pvalue for h in higher]
        each_p = [stats.ttest_rel(x, h.loc[x.index]).pvalue for h in higher]
        dish_mean = pd.concat(higher, axis=1).mean(axis=1)
        pool_u = stats.ttest_ind(x, dish_mean).pvalue
        pool_p = stats.ttest_rel(x, dish_mean.loc[x.index]).pvalue
        pool_all = stats.ttest_ind(x, pd.concat(higher)).pvalue
        above_all = bool(all(x.mean() > h.mean() for h in higher))
        sig = (max(each_u) < thr) or (pool_u < thr)
        sig_lit = (max(each_u) < thr) or (pool_all < thr)

Result: partially reproduced, resting on assumptions. At 6.63 kV/cm the 50% pulses give 198% of the unipolar mean against 35 to 68% at the higher fields, and the 100% pulses 283% against 93 to 139%, so the percent is higher at 6.7 kV/cm than at every higher field for both. For 100% the test holds (unpaired p up to 0.022 against each higher field, 0.011 against the per-dish pooled value). For 50% it does not reach p < 0.01 (p up to 0.082 against each field, 0.049 against the per-dish pooled value), so the test holds for one amplitude of two. The criterion's wording for reading (ii) pools the dish values of all higher field ROI; taken literally, every dish and ROI value pooled, it gives 50% p = 1.5e-09 and 100% p = 2.6e-09, and the outcome would be reproduced, under every variant shown. That pooling counts each dish ten times, so this attempt averages each dish over the higher field ROI first (a deviation from the criterion's letter) and the outcome is partially reproduced. The outcome depends on the ROI reading: with one side only, (b+) gives the same outcome and (b-) has neither amplitude passing (100% p = 0.078 pooled). The percentages at 6.7 kV/cm are not a measure of inhibition in the paper's sense: they exceed 100%, meaning more uptake than after unipolar pulses, because the unipolar mean there is 19 a.u. (dishes 25 and 12 a.u.), near background and smaller than the differences in background between dishes (raw YP far from the electrodes minus YP0, -7 to 127 a.u.). The 100% pass therefore rests on a ratio to a near-background unipolar mean from 2 dishes; the criterion counts it, and it is counted here.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The field of each ROI comes from an exact two dimensional solution for the electrode geometry of Methods 2.3, not the paper's finite element model; it gives 15.38 kV/cm at the centre against the paper's 15.1, and the fields are scaled to 15.1 there. ROI are contiguous 200 um squares along bb' from the centre to 3 mm, averaged over both sides (one side as variants); the paper does not give their number or spacing. YP0 and MB0 are taken in a 0.2 mm disc at the centre of each footprint. The two dishes that share one YP image are left out, so the unipolar and 25% groups have 2 dishes each. The Fig. 7 analysis uses 5 of the paper's 18 unipolar cells and 4 of its 17 bipolar cells; the pole regions are drawn here (in recordings of touching cells they include some membrane facing a neighbouring cell; leaving it out changes no result), the pulse onset is found from the data, and the cathode-facing pole is taken to be the one that brightens. Where the paper's t-test could be paired or unpaired, the unpaired test is used and the paired one shown. Where ROI values of one dish are pooled, they are averaged within the dish first, so each dish counts once. Several Fig. 2 outcomes rest on few dishes (2 unipolar dishes once the shared image is left out) and change with the ROI reading or the fit method; each section shows the variants. The 0% dishes and two of the three 25% dishes were imaged on 2021-07-29 (the third, Fig2_25_04, which shares its YP image with Fig2_0_03, on 2021-07-26), the 75% and 100% dishes on 2021-08-24, and three of the five 50% dishes on 2021-07-26, with footprint backgrounds that differ by day (mean YP0 209 to 273 a.u.), so comparisons between amplitudes are also comparisons between days. In these dishes the 100% bipolar pulses give 93 to 139% of the unipolar uptake between 8.7 and 15.1 kV/cm, where the paper describes them as inhibiting.

What was found about the dandisets.

  • 000489 holds only the dishes of Fig. 2 and one sample image (Fig1F). The dishes of Figs. 3 to 6 and the thermometry of Fig. 1E are not in either dandiset, so 13 of the 25 claims cannot be tested here. Dandisets 000548, 000549 and 000550 name this paper and match Figs. 3, 4 and 6 by title; the registry's list of the paper's datasets does not include them.
  • The YO-PRO-1 channel of sub-Fig2-0-03 (unipolar) and sub-Fig2-25-04 (25%) is the same image, while their MemBrite channels differ and their session dates differ (2021-07-29 and 2021-07-26): one recording deposited under two dishes. The two channels of the Fig1F sample image are also the same image.
  • The files give no pixel size, electrode positions or polarity, or ROI; the pixel size of 0.65 um is supported by the electrode spacing (4.44 to 4.66 mm, Methods 4.5 mm). The series description of the Fig. 2 files names "Channel1" for both dyes; the data show index 0 is MemBrite and index 1 YO-PRO-1. It also speaks of 144 images (12 x 12 grid) of a well of a six-well plate, where the paper describes 216 images of 35 mm dishes. The three 25% files name their series "Fig2_25" without the dish number.
  • 000448 holds 9 cells, each as two files (forward and reverse trials) counted as 18 subjects. The reverse files store frames in acquisition order (descending delay), and their response is offset by 74 frames (1.85 us) from the forward trial of the same cell (75 frames for cell24); neither is documented, nor the delay of each frame, the pole regions, or the field direction in the image. The darkest frame is the first in 10 of the 18 files, and 5 files have frames below half their median (frame 0 in 4 files, other frames in 3), consistent with failed flashes.
